title: the mudras
hook: a signet ring pressed into warm wax leaves a shape that stays after the ring is lifted

segments.voice: Yesterday closed trataka with the even gaze: one small point, then everything, seen with the same calm. Today the eyes rest, and the hands begin.

A drop of red wax falls on the fold of a letter. Someone presses a ring into it, holds it there a moment, and lifts it away. The ring is gone. The shape stays: a crest, a letter, a small picture, sharp-edged in the cooling wax. Whoever opens the letter can tell whose hand sealed it, and that nobody has opened it since. That little act, pressing a shape so that it holds, is close to the heart of today's word.
screen: `WAX ON THE FOLD OF A LETTER.` → `THE RING IS LIFTED. THE SHAPE STAYS.` → `PRESSING A SHAPE SO IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, mudra can mean a seal: a stamp, a signet, the mark it leaves. It also comes to mean a sign or a gesture. In a yoga class today, the word often points to the hands: fingers touching, palms joined. That's real, and the coming days will spend time there. But the word is bigger than the hands. Open the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, the same manual that described trataka, to its third chapter, and the mudras there are whole-body practices, named one by one. One is mahamudra, the great seal. In the text's description, in paraphrase, one heel presses in at the base of the body, the other leg stretches out, the hands take hold of the outstretched foot, and the chin is drawn down to the chest. Others in the same list are bandhas, locks: the chin drawn in at the throat, the belly drawn in and up, the root of the body gently drawn in. Another turns the body upside down. Not a finger shape among them. So why call these seals? Back to the wax. A seal does two things. It presses a shape in, and it closes something so that it stays. The hatha texts describe their mudras in the same spirit: shapes of the body that hold the breath and the attention in, rather than letting them leak away. The text also says these practices are to be learned from a teacher, and its descriptions are spare, not do-it-yourself instructions. For now the word gives a picture. Whether it's the whole body or two fingers, a mudra is a shape that holds.
screen: `MUDRA: A SEAL, A STAMP, A SIGN.` · `IN THE HATHA TEXT, THE WHOLE BODY.` · `MAHAMUDRA, AND THE LOCKS.` · `A SHAPE PRESSED IN, SO IT HOLDS.` · then, large: `THE RING LIFTS. THE SHAPE STAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and rest the hands on the thighs, palms down, for a few breaths, then turn the palms up for a few breaths more and notice what changes, if anything. Choose whichever feels steadier and let the whole body settle into that shape, like a ring pressed into wax: still, sharp-edged, unhurried. If the mind wanders, come back to the shape.
The mudras. Seals: shapes of the hands or of the whole body, pressed in so that something holds.
Your line: a seal pressed into wax. The ring lifts, and the shape stays. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In hatha yoga, mudras such as mahamudra and the bandhas are learned from a teacher as whole-body practices; in meditation, worship and dance, mudras are shapes of the hands.
